title: How access restrictions affect usage plans

opening.headline: We analyze how our usage plans will be affected and determine our level of preparedness when access to certain features is restricted due to the provider's safety judgment.
body: Next year's automation plan is based on the premise of a specific advanced model function, but what happens to the plan if the function is provided to some customers first or additional controls are attached due to the provider's safety judgment? If your plans get stuck on the spot, your schedule and your commitments to customers will falter along with them.

In this class, we will check the structure in which access restrictions occur in the frameworks of the three companies, and divide the restriction scenarios into four categories to organize the affected tasks and alternative means. Next, we explain the process of creating a preparedness plan using an example of document analysis automation, and learn the standards for judging the level of preparedness of our organization.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Distinguish between access restrictions and the impact of additional safeguards on use
We can determine the level of preparedness of our usage plans

screens.title: Our plan is to restrict access to certain features.
screens.lead:
Read one team's automation plan. It's a good idea to read it to find out what assumptions the plan relies on.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

visual.alt: A scene where the advanced function block placed on the schedule is blocked with a lock icon and the schedule blocks that follow are shaken.

paragraphs: A team created a plan to automate document analysis for the next year based on certain advanced model capabilities. The timeline includes introducing features, building automation, delivering on promises to customers, and deploying at scale.

However, what happens if the provider decides to provide the function only to some customers first or impose additional controls on general access based on safety judgments? If the first block is blocked, all subsequent blocks lose their homes. Not only is the schedule pushed back, but even the promises made to customers are shaken.
This class covers how to read the structure that creates such access restrictions and reflect that possibility in advance in your planning.

screens.outro: First, let's take a look at what our plan is.

screens.title: Have your plans factored in the possibility that your provider may limit functionality?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't be entering or submitting an answer, so think of our plan first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have your plans factored in the possibility that your provider may limit functionality?
items.answer: Most plans assume that the features available now will be available on the same terms in the future. However, the provider's framework openly states that safeguards and approaches may vary as capabilities increase. Check to see if you have even written down this possibility in your schedule or risk list.

items.prompt: Are there alternative models or alternative procedures?
items.answer: Alternatives come in many forms, such as previous generation models, manual procedures, and other suppliers. Any means can only be considered an alternative if it can actually be converted. A tool that only has a name and has never been used may not work when you need it.

items.prompt: How will anyone know if access is restricted?
items.answer: Restrictions may begin quietly. Even if responses are rejected or delayed, it is easy to regard them as temporary errors in the field. A person should be appointed to check the provider's announcements and policy changes and inform affected personnel.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at the plan, let's take a look at how access restrictions are structured.

screens.title: Structure that restricts access
screens.lead: Selecting an item will expand the portion of each company's framework that is associated with access restrictions. Find the direction that the three companies have in common.

items.title: OpenAI: Sufficient safeguards must be in place before deployment
items.body: Systems that reach High capability in the Preparedness Framework must have safeguards in place to sufficiently reduce the associated risk of extreme harm before deployment. A Safety Advisory Group (SAG) reviews the sufficiency of safeguards and management makes the final decision. If it is determined not to be sufficient, distribution may be withheld or limited.

items.title: Anthropic: Check current policies and risk judgments
items.body: As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

items.title: Google: Review safety practices before launch
items.body: In the Frontier Safety Framework, once Critical Competency Level (CCL) is reached, safety cases are reviewed prior to external release. This review influences the scope and terms of the release, as it means that a release will not proceed until the review passes the analysis showing that the risk has been reduced to a manageable level.

items.title: The actual structure shown by the risk report
items.body: Anthropic's risk report outlines a structure in which the strongest models will be offered to select customers first, while versions with additional safeguards will be available separately for general access. This is a practical example that shows that who uses a model and under what conditions can vary depending on ability and risk.

items.title: three common directions
items.body: All three companies point in the direction that higher capabilities can lead to different approaches and additional controls. Therefore, access restrictions are not a unilateral whim of the provider, but are the result of published thresholds and safeguard structures. Knowing the structure allows us to read in advance which signals are precursors of restriction.

screens.outro: Now that we have the structure in place, let's organize by scenario how the limitations translate into real-world work.

screens.title: Impact by restriction scenario
screens.lead: The table below outlines four scenarios where access restrictions occur, their respective impacts, and how to prepare. Please read on and guess which scenario our work is most vulnerable to.

data.caption: Contrast with restricted access scenarios
rows: A. Available to selected customers first
You can't use new features right away and have to wait or operate with a previous generation model
Maintain procedures for operating with the previous generation model and reflect the introduction time with margin in the schedule
B. Application of additional safety devices
Monitoring and access control may result in increased response rejections or delays.
Establish alternate processing procedures for channels and people to handle rejection responses.
C. Reduce the scope of use of certain competency areas
Some of the work that uses the functions of that area may be interrupted.
Prepare a list of affected tasks and manual procedures or alternative supplier alternatives.
D. Change in threshold definition due to policy revision
Affected features may change, so you may need to recheck your usage plans
Record policy versions and confirmation dates and double-check the affected functionality when changes are made
data.notes: For each scenario, write down the affected tasks, alternative means, and who will be notified. The scenarios in the table are typical types drawn from the structures described in provider documentation; which scenarios actually occur will vary depending on the provider and feature. Scenarios A and B are a matter of introduction timing and response processing method, while C and D are a matter of the scope of the work itself being different. The first two can be absorbed through schedules and procedures, but the latter two must be given high priority because work will stop if there is no alternative. Classify your work first.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the scenario, let's apply it to the case and create a preparedness plan.

screens.title: Commentary: Impact of access restrictions on business planning
screens.lead: The instructor provides step-by-step explanations of document analysis automation cases. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: Automating document analysis relies on certain advanced features. This capability determines the quality of our work in extracting and summarizing key provisions from contracts. Let's take a step-by-step look at what happens when access to this feature is restricted.

steps.title: Step 1: List dependent features
steps.body: Write down, one by one, which functions your work depends on. You should write down not only the model name, but also functional units, such as the ability to process long documents at once, tool calls, and specific output formats. Not knowing the dependent features is the lowest level of contrast.

steps.title: Step 2: Identify applicable limiting scenarios
steps.body: Indicate which of Scenarios A through D each feature in the list is vulnerable to. For example, a newer feature may be available to some customers first, which would be an A, and adding monitoring for response quality could be a B. The tasks affected will vary depending on the scenario.

steps.title: Step 3: Have an alternative plan
steps.body: We prepare how to operate under the previous generation model, how to manually handle human processes, and how to move to another supplier. You can make your choice faster if you check and write down whether each alternative actually works and how long it takes to convert.

steps.title: Step 4: Avoid single dependence
steps.body: Don’t make that feature the only vehicle for scheduling and customer commitments. Leave some leeway in the promised delivery date or quality level, or write down conditions in contracts and plans that can be fulfilled by alternative methods in case of functional limitations.

steps.title: Instructor's Summary
steps.body: You can't prevent access restrictions, but you can prepare for them. Knowing your dependencies, mapping out scenarios, preparing alternatives, and avoiding single dependencies means your planning won't stop when restrictions hit.

screens.outro: Now that we have solved the case, let’s look at the criteria for judging our organization’s level of preparedness.

screens.title: Commentary: Determining your level of preparedness
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how what you need changes as you go from low to high contrast.

stops.body: You don't know which features you depend on. Because it is not organized which tasks depend on which functions, it is not clear where access is restricted and which areas are affected. The first thing to do in this case is to create a list of dependable features for each task.

I know the dependent function, but there is no alternative. I know where I might get stuck, but there is no way to continue working when I get stuck. The next challenge is preparing to actually switch between legacy models, manual processes, and other providers.

Dependent features, limiting scenarios, fallbacks, and notification responsibilities are well documented. There are even restrictions on who checks and notifies limit signals, so you can switch right away when something changes. This document is updated whenever the policy version changes.

The framework document is publicly available, so read your provider's safety criteria regularly to compare them with your plan. As the definition of risk areas and thresholds change, the affected functions may change. Recording the date and results of comparison will serve as a starting point for the next inspection. It is easy to implement if you set the inspection cycle and person in charge, and set one specific task every quarter to raise the level of preparedness.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: Functions may be limited by the provider's safety judgment
screens.lead: Let's tie the contents of this lesson into the principles of planning. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: The provider's framework publicly commits that safeguards and approaches may vary as capabilities increase. So assuming that the features you use now will be available under the same conditions in the future is a hidden risk in planning.

Restrictions may come in the form of being offered to some customers first, adding additional safeguards, reducing availability, or changing standards as policy changes are made. For each scenario, writing down the affected tasks, alternative means, and who will be notified will speed up your response.

The key to preparedness is to start with knowing your dependencies, have a fallback plan, and avoid single dependencies. Incorporate this principle into your schedule and customer appointments as well. Since the provider's documents are public, the cheapest way to prepare is to read them regularly and compare them with your own plans.

Finally, transfer the standards from this lesson into your organization's documents. All you have to do is add functional restriction items to the risk list, create a table listing dependent functions, alternative means, and notification personnel for each task, and determine the frequency of checking provider documents. If you have that ticket, when you hear about the restrictions, the discussion doesn't start from scratch, it starts with updating the ticket.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Access restrictions are not a unilateral whim of the provider, but arise from an open structure. If you know the structure, you can predict it, and if you can predict it, you can prepare.

checks.intro: Apply the scenario table. Just choose the response that best suits the situation. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The advanced features our automation plans depend on are being made available to some customers first and we are second to none. What is the most appropriate response?
options: The provider will release it, so leave the plan as is.
Schedule is halted even if there is an alternative to operating with the previous generation model
Assume that the general access version is exactly the same as the priority delivery model.
Stand by or operate with previous generation models and note down the impact tasks and notification responsibilities.
checks.correctFeedback: First, we chose exactly the response that suited our delivery scenario.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This response is a choice that does not reflect possible limitations or uses no alternatives.
checks.explain: In some customer priority delivery scenarios, you may want to wait or operate with the previous generation model. For each scenario, you should note the affected tasks, alternative means, and who will be notified.

wrong.0: If you don't factor the possibility of functional limitations into your plans, your schedule will falter.
wrong.1: If you have alternative means, you can continue your work.
wrong.2: It should be assumed that approaches and additional controls may vary.

checks.intro: Think about the order of the case explanations. All you need to do is put the four steps in the right order to create a preparedness plan.
checks.q: Make sure you have a plan in place to prepare for access restrictions.
items: Make a list of dependent features
Point out the applicable restriction scenarios A to D.
Have alternative plans in place, such as older models, manual procedures, or different suppliers.
Avoid making the function a single dependency on schedules and customer commitments
checks.correctFeedback: We got the order right from grasp to reflection.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Consider that you need to know what you depend on so you can figure out the scenario, and you need alternative means to reflect it in your promises.
checks.explain: After identifying the dependent functions, identify the corresponding scenario, prepare alternative means, and reflect it in the schedule and appointment.

glossary.def: Capabilities and risks limit the targets and scope of functions provided. This appears in the form of preferential provision to some customers or a reduction in the scope of use.
These are protection measures that go beyond the basic level, such as monitoring and access control. This can affect your user experience in the form of increased rejections or delays.
It is an alternative to continue work when a function cannot be used. There are older generation models, manual procedures, and different suppliers.
It's about building the possibility of limited functionality into schedules and customer commitments.

misconceptions.myth: The functions you use now can be used in the future under the same conditions.
misconceptions.fact: Approaches and additional controls may vary depending on the provider's safety judgment. Even for models in the same series, priority provision and general access conditions may be different.

misconceptions.myth: Access restrictions are at the unilateral whim of the provider.
misconceptions.fact: Limitations come from the threshold and safeguard structures of the published framework. By reading the document, you can find out in advance under what conditions the restrictions will occur.

misconceptions.myth: Alternative means are only needed in the event of a major accident.
misconceptions.fact: Even during normal operation, functional limitations or policy revisions may occur, requiring alternative means. You should check the possibility of conversion on a regular basis so you can use it when you need it.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Features may be restricted by the provider's safety judgment.
Restrictions come in the form of preferential offers to some customers, additional safeguards, reduced scope of use, and policy revisions.
Knowing your dependent features and having a fallback plan can help you be prepared.
Avoid single reliance on schedules and customer commitments.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where do we have the greatest single-function dependencies in our work, and what can we do to prepare there? Also think about whether you have ever actually used an alternative method.
